Regenera Deià is an initiative to regenerate the town of
Deià through an integrated approach to agriculture, water management, forest
stewardship, wildfire prevention, and community resilience. Its goal is to foster a
territory that is more vibrant, resilient, and self-sustaining.

Regenera Deià emerged in response to a very specific urgency: the growing threat of
devastating wildfires in the region. From that starting point, the project has expanded to
focus on prevention, land stewardship, and rethinking how the territory is managed —
placing the community at the centre of the process. Its vision is to transform risk into
opportunity, strengthening resilience while reactivating the rural economy.

Regenera Deià works holistically to realign people and place, economy and nature. It
seeks to regenerate the land, strengthen the community, and revitalise the rural economy
— recognising that long-term resilience depends on restoring balance between
ecological health, local livelihoods, and social cohesion.
What does it actually do on the ground?

Regenera Deià is creating critical firebreaks, reactivating local agriculture and forestry,
strengthening water resilience, and mobilising the community around long-term land
stewardship.

Regenera Deià was launched in 2025 as an open and collaborative initiative led by
Fundació Iniciatives del Mediterrani (FIM), with the initial support of the local
association Abocaverds, Tramuntana XXI, Save the Med, Mallorca Preservation
Foundation, and a broad network of public and private partners.
It is a non-profit initiative designed to empower the community through active
participation and shared ownership of the projects and initiatives it develops.
What is the relationship between Regenera Deià and the Deià Town Hall?

Regenera Deià is not part of the Ajuntament de Deià, nor is it funded, directed, or managed by the town hall. It is an independent non-profit initiative led by FIM and Abocaverds, developed in collaboration with a broad network of public and private partners.
At the same time, Regenera Deià works closely with the Ajuntament and with other relevant institutions to support existing efforts, strengthen coordination, and help address critical gaps where public administrations may lack the resources, capacity, or flexibility to act alone. The relationship is therefore one of collaboration and complementarity: Regenera Deià seeks to add value, mobilise support, and contribute practical capacity towards a shared goal of making Deià more resilient, regenerative, and self-sustaining.

You can join the movement by attending our community gatherings, volunteering your
time and skills, supporting the initiative through a donation, or sharing your ideas with
us.
Follow us on Instagram, subscribe to our mailing list, give us a call, come to one of our
events, or stop by our office to say hello — we’d love to connect.
What kind of activities do we organize

We believe in the power of a community coming together to share and nurture its love
for the land. That’s why we host a full calendar of activities, including walks, talks,
gastronomic gatherings, clean-ups, and a community garden where everyone is
welcome.
What can i do as a property owner?

As a property owner, you can count on us to help you access available funding, navigate
planning permissions and administrative processes, and connect with trusted suppliers
and professionals. Our goal is to support you in managing your land in the most
environmentally responsible and cost-effective way possible.

The ultimate goal of Regenera Deià is to transform the town into a living model of
holistic regeneration — where ecological health, a thriving rural economy, and a strong,
connected community reinforce one another. It seeks to build long-term resilience by
restoring balance between land, livelihoods, and local wellbeing.

Deià is uniquely positioned to become a model for regenerative action. As a UNESCO
cultural landscape within the Serra de Tramuntana, it combines extraordinary natural
value with deep-rooted agricultural and cultural traditions. At the same time, it faces
real challenges — wildfire risk, water vulnerability, rural decline, and economic
pressure. These challenges make Deià not only a place in need of regeneration, but a
place capable of leading it.

Regenera Deià is funded through a combination of private donations, foundation grants,
public funding and earned revenue. As a non-profit initiative, all funds are reinvested
directly into land stewardship, community projects, and the development of resilient
local systems.

Community Activities, Discovering the Deia Forest with Marti Bestard | Regenera Deià

The interpretive excursions with Martí Bestard are an invitation to rediscover Deià through its paths, forests, and terraced landscapes. It is not just about walking, but about inhabiting the territory with awareness: observing it, listening to it, and understanding it. Through these guided outings, a space is created to reconnect with the surrounding landscape, experiencing it directly and gaining a deeper understanding of the challenges and opportunities that shape its present and future.

The landscape of Deià is the result of a millenary relationship between people and nature. The dry-stone terraces, the traditional paths that once connected farms and villages, and the holm oak forests that have provided resources and shelter all stand as testimony to a territory shaped with care and wisdom.

With Martí Bestard, an experienced mountain guide, these walks become an interpretive journey through this agroforestry mosaic. We will explore the historical uses of the land, the management practices that have sustained life in the Serra de Tramuntana, and the biodiversity that still inhabits these spaces today. We will also venture into the holm oak forests of Deià, discovering their ecological richness, their history, and their current state, highlighting a natural heritage that often goes unnoticed.

These excursions remind us that the landscape is not a static backdrop, but a living system that reflects human decisions and relationships over time. Walking through it with attention allows us to better understand current challenges—such as agricultural abandonment, tourism pressure, and fire risk—and to imagine new ways of coexisting with the territory.

Reconnecting with Deià is also about reconnecting with ourselves: with natural rhythms, with situated knowledge, and with a more conscious way of inhabiting the world. These outings open the door to a regenerative perspective, where the past inspires the present and paves the way toward a more resilient future.

Roig: A Regenera Deià product rooted in the land
Regenera Deià is preparing to launch its first local product:

Following its mission to restore traditional land use, reactivate agriculture and rebuild a rural economy around the landscape, Regenera Deià has begun with a simple question that many people in the village have asked themselves: how can so much fruit be wasted in a place like Deià?

Orchard after orchard, citrus trees produce lemons, oranges and mandarins, only for much of the fruit to fall to the ground and rot. Not because it lacks quality, but because local fruit can no longer compete in price with cheap imported produce.
Regenera Deià is asking a different question: what if that trend could be reversed?

Deià sits at the heart of an agricultural landscape shaped over centuries of cultivation, recognised and protected by UNESCO. Yet despite this history, there are still very few genuinely local products available to buy in the village’s shops, bars, hotels and restaurants.
Roig is the first response: Deià’s first local drink.

It is a top-grade artisanal natural bitters: a Mallorcan twist on the classic aperitif, made from local citrus and blended with artichoke leaves to create its characteristic bitter flavour. Its colour follows an older tradition, using cochineal colouring rather than the artificial shortcuts often associated with commercial mass production.
The result is something both familiar and new: an aperitif rooted in Deià’s land, fruit, orchards and agricultural memory.

Roig is also intended as an alternative to the commercial imported aperitifs that dominate the market. Instead of artificial products travelling from elsewhere, Regenera Deià wants to show that a drink of real quality can be made from the fruit already growing in the valley.

A bottle of Roig is therefore more than a drink. It is a small experiment in regeneration: a way of giving value back to local fruit, supporting land stewardship, reducing waste and proving that the landscape can once again produce culture, economy and pleasure.
If Deià is to remain a living landscape rather than a postcard, its fields, orchards and terraces must have a future. Roig is one first step in that direction.
Roig has been designed above all to restore value to the land.
The lemons, oranges and mandarins used for the first production have been kindly donated from three unique family orchards across Deià:
The Swarovski family’s hundred-year-old orchard east of Deià, in the Son Beltran area.
The Lloyd-Webber family’s orchard in the heart of the village.
Sandra and Tony’s unique new orchard on the easternmost cliffs of Deià.
Together, these orchards tell a story of place: old trees, renewed cultivation, family stewardship, and the possibility of bringing agricultural value back into the village economy.

All revenues from the sales of this product will be reinvested in agricultural reactivation. The aim is to plant more fruit trees, herbs and vegetables, expand the local offer, and develop more products rooted in Deià’s land.

Thanks to this collaboration, Regenera Deià has been able to produce a high-quality local drink in record time. More than a bottle, it is a practical attempt to reverse a century-long trend of agricultural abandonment by creating value from what Deià’s land already produces.

Deià Revolving Solidarity Fund | Regenera Deià
Regenera Deià Launches Its Revolving Solidarity Fund

In Deià, caring for the landscape means far more than preserving a beautiful view. It means keeping olive groves alive, restoring agricultural land, managing forests, reducing wildfire risk, and supporting the people who have cared for this territory for generations.
As we mark our first year of activity, Regenera Deià is taking an important new step with the launch of our
, a tool designed to help small landowners access public grants for wildfire prevention and the restoration of agricultural landscapes.

The fund was created to solve a simple but critical problem: many public grants require landowners to pay the full cost of the work upfront before they can claim reimbursement. For those without sufficient liquidity, this requirement can turn an approved grant into an opportunity they simply cannot access.
We want to close that gap.
When Funding Exists but Cannot Be Used

In the Serra de Tramuntana, a range of grant programmes can finance essential work, including the restoration of traditional olive groves through pine removal, land clearance, and the rehabilitation of agricultural features.

These interventions deliver benefits that extend far beyond a single property. They help bring productive land back into use, encourage more active land stewardship, and reduce the continuous vegetation that allows wildfires to spread.
However, the structure of many grant schemes presents a major obstacle: the work must first be completed and paid for before reimbursement can be claimed.

For a small landowner, advancing several thousand euros can be impossible. As a result, some of the people with the deepest connection to the land, and the strongest commitment to its conservation, are excluded from the very support intended to help them.

"Too often, the people who most deserve these grants, and who have demonstrated the greatest commitment to the landscape over many years, are precisely those who cannot access them," says Joe Holles de Peyer, Director of Regenera Deià.
How the Revolving Solidarity Fund Works
The fund will provide the upfront capital needed to carry out projects that have been approved, or are expected to qualify, for public funding.
Once the work has been completed and the grant has been paid, the advanced capital returns to the fund and can be used to support another property and another restoration project.
That is why it is called a revolving fund. A single contribution does not generate impact just once. It can be reused repeatedly, multiplying its impact over time.
The model connects three key elements:
Small landowners committed to caring for their land.
Public funding available for landscape restoration.
Philanthropic contributions that unlock access to those public grants.

For donors, this creates an especially effective model. Their contribution does not replace public funding. Instead, it enables it. Every euro donated can unlock additional public resources before returning to the fund to support another project.
"For philanthropists, contributing to a fund that unlocks additional public financing represents an especially effective and attractive model," says Holles de Peyer.

The Revolving Solidarity Fund is not a standalone initiative. It builds upon the pilot landowner support service that Regenera Deià has developed during its first year, through which our team has already visited more than 30 properties across the municipality.
Every property faces different challenges. Some need help identifying suitable grants. Others require support with administrative procedures, project planning, or finding qualified contractors.
Our goal is to accompany landowners throughout the entire process, from identifying needs and funding opportunities to overseeing work on the ground.

Limited liquidity is a major barrier, but it is not the only one. Bureaucracy, complex application procedures, and the difficulty of finding specialist professionals can all prevent projects from moving forward. That is why we combine financing, technical guidance, and implementation support.
Restoring the Landscape Mosaic That Once Protected the Territory
This work forms part of a broader vision: restoring Deià's traditional agroforestry mosaic.

For centuries, the landscape consisted of a diverse mix of olive groves, orchards, pastureland, and actively managed woodland. Sheep grazing helped control vegetation, olive groves remained productive, farmland stayed open, and forests provided timber, fuel, and building materials.

The gradual abandonment of these traditional activities has encouraged the expansion of continuous woodland and the accumulation of combustible vegetation. At a time of increasing wildfire risk, restoring a diverse, productive, and actively managed landscape is also a strategy for protecting it.
Our aim is not to recreate the past, but to build on its lessons. We seek to combine traditional knowledge with new models of financing, collaboration, and local entrepreneurship.
A First Year of Turning Ideas into Action
The launch of the Revolving Solidarity Fund follows an exceptionally active first year.
Thanks to more than €300,000 in philanthropic contributions, Regenera Deià has helped establish three strategic firebreaks across the municipality and launched its landowner support service.
We have also developed projects that connect landscape regeneration with economic and cultural activity. These include
, a bitter aperitif made from locally sourced fruit, as well as a furniture collection created in collaboration with Amarar and the Manacor-based woodworking company Germans Adrover.
These initiatives sit alongside community dinners, a community garden, and support for the local theatre group.
Although these projects may appear diverse, they are all driven by the same belief: a living landscape depends on an active community and a local economy rooted in the territory.
An Investment That Can Be Used Again and Again
The Revolving Solidarity Fund represents a new approach to local philanthropy.

Rather than financing a single one-off intervention, contributions create a shared financial infrastructure. A fund that enables work to begin, unlocks public grants, and then recovers its capital so the process can start again.

A restored property can mean a recovered olive grove, reduced forest fuel loads, increased agricultural activity, employment for local professionals, and a landscape that is more resilient to wildfire.
When that same capital is then used to support another property, its impact continues to grow.
This is the principle that guides the fund: making one project possible today so that it can help finance another tomorrow.
We are looking for landowners, partners, and donors who share our commitment to caring for Deià through practical, long-term solutions that multiply their impact.
Anyone interested in applying for support, contributing to the fund, or learning more about how it works is warmly invited to get in touch with Regenera Deià.
Ecoacoustics · Listening to Deià’s biodiversity | Regenera Deià

Regenera Deià is working with Rampa Lab to listen to the territory in a new way. Rampa Lab is the creative and scientific laboratory through which Jaume Reus, a musician, producer and environmental scientist specialised in ecoacoustics, and Laia Malo, a musician, translator and poet, explore language, music and non-human environments, especially natural soundscapes.

Their work begins from the idea that art is the language of bonds and collective identities, and that it is not exclusive to human beings. Through art-science projects, sound art, performances and workshops, they combine scientific rigour with an appreciation for local heritage and a commitment to sharing knowledge beyond conventional academic settings.

In Deià, Rampa Lab has been carrying out a campaign of field recordings for Regenera Deià, documenting birds, insects, amphibians, wind, water and seasonal soundscapes. These recordings will help establish an acoustic biodiversity baseline, allowing the project to track the effects of conservation and regeneration work over time while making the ecological life of the village audible, emotional and accessible.

On 6 June, Jaume and Laia shared the first results of their fieldwork in an outstanding live performance and presentation attended by around 40 neighbours. Combining the sounds recorded across the municipality with live music and a poetry recital, they transformed scientific findings into a collective cultural experience, revealing the hidden voices of Deià’s landscape.

Their early observations point to a rich and active soundscape, with notable signs of pollinator activity, especially around the municipality’s vegetable gardens, including the community garden. The project also opens the door to future collaborations with local and visiting musicians, who may use Deià’s recorded soundscapes as raw material for new compositions.

In this way, ecoacoustics becomes more than a monitoring tool. It becomes a bridge between science, art and community: a way of listening to biodiversity, reconnecting culture with ecology, and reminding the village that regeneration also begins with attention.
Firebreak Furniture: Turning Forest Risk into Regenerative Value | Regenera Deià
From fire prevention to local production
Regenera Deià is built around a simple but ambitious idea: turning challenges into opportunities, and risk into value.

The project began with one of the most urgent threats facing Deià and the Serra de Tramuntana: the growing danger of forest fires. Years of land abandonment, reduced rural activity and changing climate conditions have increased the need for active forest management.
The challenge is not only to reduce fire risk, but also to rebuild a rural economy capable of keeping forests healthy, safe and productive.
For Regenera Deià, a firebreak is therefore more than an emergency measure. It is also a potential source of material, employment, craft and future value.

Forest interventions produce wood and other natural resources. Rather than allowing this material to go to waste, the project aims to honour the trees that must be felled by transforming them into something lasting, useful and beautiful.
This is the idea behind Regenera Deià’s limited-edition line of firebreak furniture.
Each piece tells the story of the landscape it comes from: a forest made safer, material recovered from abandonment, local craftsmanship supported and an economy reconnecting with the land.

By transforming wood from fire-prevention work into furniture, Regenera Deià aims to create products that generate income for further land management. Firebreaks produce material, material becomes design, design creates revenue, and that revenue helps fund new firebreaks.
It is a practical model of regeneration in which resilience, beauty and economic value reinforce one another.
The first key partner in this process was the local design studio Amarar, which has been working to reactivate a forestry sector weakened by decades of decline.

Its contribution is not limited to design. It also involves recovering traditional knowledge: cutting wood at the right time, soaking it to stabilise the grain, curing it slowly and working it with patience and precision.
These techniques were once part of rural life but risk disappearing as forests become unmanaged and local production declines.
Through this collaboration, Regenera Deià and Amarar are exploring how traditional forestry knowledge can become part of a contemporary regenerative economy.

Grazing for Resilient Landscapes | Regenera Deià
Two years ago, a small herd of goats moved back into Deià's abandoned pastures. Today, they are one of the valley's most effective tools against wildfire.

When people think about wildfire prevention, they often imagine fire trucks, helicopters and emergency response teams. Yet for most of Mediterranean history, one of the most effective preventive tools walked on four legs.

Inspired by the Catalan initiative Ramats de Foc, Regenera Deià began its own grazing project two years ago. We gave a small herd of goats a home, started clearing our own land and our neighbours', and built a routine: grazing every evening, during the last three hours before sunset, moving through abandoned areas, properties and paths. It is largely a practice of observation — reading the land, going where it is most needed, giving plants time to recover. Giving something back to the ecosystem we are part of is central to why we do it.

Grazing animals — goats, sheep, donkeys — were once essential to a well-managed Tramuntana landscape. They were not only a source of food, wool and income; they were active land managers, cared for because they sustained life, not because they were passive assets. Moving across terraces, forest edges and mountain slopes, they consumed the vegetation that would otherwise accumulate as fuel, helping maintain the mosaic that defined the Serra for centuries.

Much of that grazing activity has since disappeared. As tourism drew people away from traditional agriculture, rural populations shrank and grazing areas were abandoned. Shrubs expanded, young pine forest spread into old farmland, and vegetation grew denser. The result is a landscape carrying far more continuous fuel than it once did — a change with consequences well beyond fire risk: dense vegetation competes for scarce water, reduces habitat diversity, and in many places is pushing out the open ground that pollinators, birds and native plants depend on.

Reintroducing grazing is one of the most effective and natural ways to address these challenges. At Regenera Deià, the concept of Guerrilla Grazing explores how carefully managed animals can once again become partners in landscape regeneration.

This approach is increasingly recognised across southern Europe, as conservationists, foresters and fire specialists rediscover what rural communities once understood intuitively: animals can do ecological work that is difficult, expensive, or simply impossible to replicate with technology alone.

But Guerrilla Grazing is about more than vegetation. It raises a broader question about the future of rural economies. If grazing becomes economically viable again, it can support local farmers, create new livelihoods, and strengthen the connection between communities and the landscapes they inhabit. Grazing, in other words, is not simply a conservation tool — it is part of a wider regenerative strategy that links ecology, culture and economy, and healthy landscapes need care that is backed by activities capable of sustaining themselves over time.
Zooming In: Guerrilla Grazing in Deià

The name guerrilla grazing provokes all kinds of reactions the first time people hear it — from images of jungle warfare, to tropical gorillas, to weariness at yet another trendy label for a practice that has existed for millennia. Whatever your first reaction, what matters to us is what you think of our approach to caring for Deià's abandoned land.

It is not simply a way of making use of poor pasture or managing spontaneous vegetation with animals. It is a way of keeping our forests safer, helping biodiversity thrive, and preserving an ancestral farming heritage — a modern name for a practice that emerged, quite simply, from the need to act.

Three years ago, ABOCA Verds was born from that same urgency: olive groves left unmanaged had gradually become fire-prone pine forest, and a young couple felt the pull to do something about it, with the hope of one day producing a good goat cheese along the way. While we wait for our goats to be ready to milk, they are already doing essential work managing the pine understory on the western side of the municipality.
Two weeks ago, our first flock of Ovella Roja Mallorquina — the native Majorcan sheep breed — arrived, bringing a second, complementary set of grazing habits to the guerrilla.

The guerrilla in the name refers to carrying out occasional, targeted grazing interventions wherever and whenever they are most needed. We concentrate our animals on the plots we judge to require the most urgent management: land alongside public and private paths, streams and roads, where fire risk is highest.

This high-intensity, carefully managed technique benefits both land and people. It reduces the dense shrub understory, helps restore balance between vegetation layers — supporting biodiversity — allows pasture to recover instead of degrading through overgrazing, contributes to carbon sequestration, and helps prevent soil erosion and water evaporation. As a bonus, the animals disperse seeds, conveniently packaged in their own natural fertiliser.

And here is our best-kept secret: the animals love it. Constant access to fresh, varied vegetation improves their health and wellbeing, and reduces our need to import forage from elsewhere on the island — or the mainland — as well as our dependence on commercial feed.

Guerrilla grazing is a land management technique that is sadly disappearing, as extensive livestock farming declines and industrial models take its place. Extensive, conscious, rotational grazing systems that respect animal welfare are becoming rare, and with them, the traditional knowledge, skills and rural culture that once surrounded them. This is one of the reasons we believe it is so important to bring this way of caring for the land back.

One of the newest additions to our guerrilla is invisible fencing technology. Our herds wear GPS collars, which let us create and move virtual grazing areas without building permanent fences — giving us the flexibility to respond quickly to changing conditions and direct the herd precisely where their work is needed most, while minimising disturbance to the landscape. For us, the collars do not replace good shepherding; they are another tool that helps us manage the land more effectively, improve animal welfare through adaptive grazing, and make this traditional practice viable again in the 21st century.

One of the collars' greatest advantages is the ability to create exclusion zones within a grazing area — virtual boundaries that protect young trees, dry-stone terraces, sensitive habitats or any feature of ecological or cultural value, while the animals continue grazing freely around them. This precision makes conservation and grazing fully compatible, and the flexibility of virtual fencing lets us expand guerrilla grazing across the municipality: rather than one large herd in a single place, we can rotate several smaller herds at once, targeting priority areas as conditions shift through the year. The result is faster response to fire risk, more efficient vegetation management, and a better balance between grazing pressure and ecosystem recovery.

We, as humans, need to relearn that we are not the centre of the world — that slowing down is, in many ways, the answer to the interconnected problems we face, and that managing an ecosystem from within means understanding ourselves as part of it. Deià's future resilience depends on this understanding: on what we build, and on what we are willing to bring back.
Growing Community: The Role of Community Gardens in Regenera Deià | Regenera Deià
From a handful of raised beds in an open field to the first seed of a much larger agricultural future.

There are many reasons why someone joins a community garden. But before any of them comes a simpler idea: an open space, a shared space, a place for conversation and collective creation. Somewhere between private and public, people gather to bring ideas, skills and motivation into growing something new, together.

It is perhaps no surprise that people so often describe gardening and writing as closely related practices. Both require patience, attention, cultivation and care — for ideas, for people, and for the environments we inhabit. Community gardens are not simply about growing vegetables, nor are they a distraction from environmental and political crises. Building Community: Weaving Practice, Theory and People

A resilient community is not built through infrastructure or economic activity alone, but through relationships — between neighbours, generations, cultures and the land itself. For centuries, food production was woven into everyday life in Deià. Gardens, orchards and terraces were not only sources of nourishment; they were places of knowledge, cooperation and cultural continuity. Today, much of that connection has faded. Agricultural knowledge is disappearing, productive land is being abandoned, and food increasingly arrives from far beyond the island.

Community gardens offer a way to restore these relationships. More than places to grow vegetables, they are shared spaces where people cultivate food, exchange knowledge, care for the land and build connections across generations and backgrounds. They transform underused land into productive commons that strengthen biodiversity, improve soil health, reconnect people with seasonal cycles, and encourage participation in the stewardship of the local landscape.

Their value extends beyond ecological restoration. In times of social fragmentation, economic uncertainty and environmental crisis, community gardens strengthen local resilience by creating opportunities for cooperation, mutual learning and collective responsibility. They remind us that regeneration is not carried out by experts alone, but is a practice rooted in everyday acts of participation and care.

Seen this way, a community garden is not simply a place. It is a living practice of reciprocity, stewardship and belonging — a small but tangible expression of the regenerative future we are cultivating together.

The Es Jonquet Community Gardens are much more than a place to grow vegetables or meet people from the village. They are a living learning space, where neighbours share knowledge, learn from one another's successes and mistakes, explore new growing methods, and, most importantly, put into practice what they learn by experimenting on their own plots.

This philosophy is rooted in experiential learning: the idea that knowledge is best acquired through direct experience. More than a century ago, the Mallorcan educator Guillem Cifre de Colonya championed exactly this — that education should cultivate autonomy, curiosity and practical skill rather than simply transmit information. We believe learning by doing remains the most effective way to build lasting knowledge and confidence.

ABOCA Verds, which coordinates and manages the community gardens, organises monthly workshops and courses on organic growing, permaculture, soil health, composting, water management, seed saving, agroforestry and other regenerative land-use practices, led both by members of the association and by invited farmers, educators and practitioners. The sessions are open to everyone — not only plot holders, but neighbours, local growers and anyone curious about a more conscious relationship with the land.

Beyond the practical knowledge, these gatherings create space for spontaneous conversation, exchange and connection. In a small rural community, these informal networks are as valuable as the vegetables we harvest — they are what build a more resilient, cooperative community with a renewed culture of care, for people and for land alike.

When we look at the road ahead, the first impulse is to dream big — of abundant landscapes, thriving communities and ambitious projects. And rightly so: that is where the best ideas begin. But it is equally important to keep our roots firmly in the ground, and move forward patiently, seed by seed, terrace by terrace.

Thanks to the generosity and trust of the landowners, who have granted the use of the property to Regenera Deià, we are delighted to announce that the first seed has already been planted. It is now quietly taking root, ready to grow into something much bigger.

Next steps include restoring several collapsed dry-stone terraces and securing the property's perimeter fencing — essential measures to bring this corner of the village back into active cultivation and allow the project to grow beyond the current community garden. The fencing matters because the herds of feral goats that roam the area can undo months of work in a single night. The terraces matter because dry-stone walls prevent erosion, slow the run-off of rainwater and help the soil hold on to moisture — all critical to the land's long-term recovery.

This vote of confidence in Regenera Deià reflects the success of the community gardens and the wider vision for the landscape that has grown around them. It opens the door to a new phase of agricultural regeneration on the property. Technical details of the expansion — cultivation models, land-use strategy — will follow, always in close collaboration with the landowners.

The principles behind these gardens will guide every step of this next chapter. The ambition is to build a living laboratory for regenerative agriculture, education and landscape restoration — not only for Deià, but for the wider Serra de Tramuntana. Beyond producing healthy food and strengthening community ties, the site will show how regenerative practices can help growers build more diverse, productive and drought-resilient plots, improve biodiversity, restore soil health, and adapt to a changing climate.

A garden begins with a single seed, a shared plot, a handful of neighbours willing to show up. What grows from it is education, biodiversity and a community that trusts itself to shape its own future.

Recipes for Regeneration: Reviving the Taste of Deià | Regenera Deià

A landscape is not only trees, terraces and paths. It is also the food people make from what the land gives, the memories attached to every dish, and the knowledge passed down around kitchen tables. For Regenera Deià, restoring the valley’s agriculture and ecology has always gone hand in hand with restoring what that land is actually cooked into — the sopes, the sobrassada, the fish stews that once brought a whole household to the table.

Food as memory, food as landscape

Traditional Deià cooking was never separate from the land around it. It depended on what the terraces, orchards and coastline produced each season, and it carried, in every recipe, generations of knowledge about how to use it well: how to stretch ingredients, respect produce, and turn a handful of what was available into a meal that could gather a household together.

Much of that knowledge lives today only in the memory of the village’s elders. Regenera Deià’s culinary programme exists to make sure it does not stop there — to create spaces where that knowledge can pass naturally from one generation to the next, before it is lost.

So far, Regenera Deià has organised three gastronomic gatherings built around exactly this idea: cooking together, across generations, nationalities and backgrounds, guided by the village’s own elders and produce.

The first was a Sopes Deianenques evening, followed soon after by a Sobrassada workshop at Can Vallés last winter. Each gathering has followed the same spirit: an elder explaining how a dish was made fifty years ago, a group of neighbours and visitors learning by doing, and a shared meal at the end of it.
These events have quickly become one of Regenera Deià’s most loved traditions, and the project intends to keep building on them: more dishes, more elders, more generations at the same table.

Regenera Deià works closely with local chef Lluís Ferrer, who has led all three gatherings to date. Lluís brings the skill of a professional kitchen, but just as importantly, the humility to listen — knowing that an elder explaining how a dish was made fifty years ago may hold as much wisdom as any formal recipe.

His involvement with Regenera Deià goes beyond these gatherings. Lluís has also been closely involved in the development of Roig, Regenera Deià’s first local product: an artisanal bitters made from Deià citrus. His input has helped shape a drink that, like the workshops themselves, turns what the land already produces into something the whole village can share and be proud of.

It is this combination — a chef rooted in the village, working alongside neighbours who still remember how things used to be done — that makes the programme work. Lluís does not treat Deià’s food as a museum piece to be preserved behind glass. He lets it breathe, adapts it, and helps carry it forward.

Recovering a recipe is a small act. But multiplied across a village, across seasons, across generations, these small acts add up to something larger: a community that still knows how to feed itself from its own land, and that trusts its own knowledge enough to pass it on.

This is why Regenera Deià treats gastronomy as part of the same regenerative work as its forests, its water and its fields. A restored terrace matters more when someone still knows what to cook with what grows on it. A recovered orchard matters more when its fruit ends up, once again, in a pot on a Deià stove.
Deià’s food was never meant to sit still. It grew out of what the land gave and the people who knew how to use it — and, gathering by gathering, it is learning to do that again.

Together, these measures form part of a coherent forest management strategy that combines wildfire prevention, recovery of the agroforestry mosaic, and the reactivation of the primary sector as key pillars of a long-term regenerative approach.
A regeneration model emerging from the community

Regenera Deià was created with the ambition of turning the municipality into a Mediterranean reference for territorial regeneration. The project integrates forest management, agricultural reactivation, water stewardship, and community engagement within a shared vision.
These first forest interventions symbolize more than technical work in the landscape. They mark the beginning of a broader process that seeks to reconnect economy, nature, and community.

More than 20 fincas visited in six months
Over the last six months, the Regenera Deià team has visited more than 20 fincas across the municipality.

Each visit is different. Some properties need urgent forest thinning to reduce wildfire risk. Others have abandoned olive groves or orchards that could be recovered. Some require help navigating administrative procedures. Others need support connecting with the right forestry teams, understanding funding opportunities, or designing a realistic land management plan.
What they all have in common is that they form part of a larger landscape.

In Deià, no finca is completely isolated. A forested plot affects the neighbouring plot. A blocked access path affects emergency response. An abandoned terrace affects erosion and water retention. A recovered olive grove can help reopen a mosaic landscape that benefits biodiversity, fire prevention, and local identity.
This is why Regenera Deià works finca by finca, but always with the whole territory in mind.
The one-stop support service helps landowners move from intention to implementation.

This includes basic land management guidance, support in identifying priority interventions, help navigating red tape, contact with technical experts and contractors, and assistance with funding applications.

So far, Regenera Deià has managed four funding applications, three of which have already been successful. These results show that many of the resources needed for better land management do exist, but accessing them requires time, coordination, and technical knowledge.
The purpose of the service is to make that process easier for landowners and more strategic for the municipality as a whole.

Deià’s landscape is beautiful, but it is also fragile. Decades of agricultural abandonment, increasing forest density, climate stress, and wildfire risk have created a situation that requires coordinated action.

Public administrations have a role to play. So do local companies, technical specialists, funders, residents, and civil society. But private landowners are essential. Over 92% of the Serra de Tramuntana is in private hands, which means that the future of the region depends on helping those landowners become active partners in regeneration.
Regenera’s one-stop support service is designed precisely for this: to remove obstacles, build trust, and help transform concern into practical action.
If you own or manage land in Deià and would like support, Regenera Deià invites you to visit the Villa Rullan office.
Regenera is open every Tuesday and Thursday from 10:00 to 14:00.
You can also contact through the website: regeneradeia.com.

Whether you are thinking about forest management, olive grove recovery, grazing, access improvement, funding, permits, or simply want to understand what is possible on your land, the service is here to help.
Because caring for Deià’s landscape cannot depend on isolated efforts alone. It needs coordination, practical support, and a shared commitment to the future of the territory.
Gastronomical Activities — Food as Culture, Nature and Family | Regenera Deià
Bringing our heritage back to the table — intergenerational recipes, community meals, and revived traditions.

Few things connect people so deeply with land and culture as food. In Deià, the gastronomical heritage is rich, and through Regenera Deià we are partnering with local guardians of that heritage to rediscover the flavours, stories, and wisdom of our culinary past.

From conversations with neighbors and research into local history, we have begun unearthing the treasured recipes of our grandmothers and great grandmothers. With visionary local chef Lluís Ferrer and masters of tradition like Magdalena X and Xisca Y, we are recreating these dishes — not as relics, but as living recipes informed by land, season and story.

Every couple of months, friends, family and neighbours gather beneath trees and beside long tables to share these meals: from traditional Sopes de Deià to Escaldums with a contemporary twist, sobrassada workshops and more. These gatherings are intergenerational — young and old, local and newcomer — and they revive a sense of belonging that only shared food and shared history can create.
These experiences go beyond taste — they are exchanges of memory, identity, and belonging.
Food isn’t just nourishment; it’s heritage distilled in flavour. In Deià, rediscovering our recipes is rediscovering our roots.
